newsitem.title: USA: Union issue threatens to keep U.S. Senate in town.
newsitem.headline: Union issue threatens to keep U.S. Senate in town.

text.p: A labour issue affecting only one company tied up the Senate in procedural knots Monday and dashed members' hopes of adjourning for the year as early as Monday night.
The problem centred on a popular bill beefing up airport construction and anti-terrorism measures that all senators wanted enacted.
But pro-labour senators, who had the ability to block the bill at least temporarily, wanted it shorn of a measure that applied just to the Federal Express Corp.

These senators said the provision, quietly inserted into the bill as a technical correction, was designed to help FedEx in "union-busting" efforts. Supporters of the provision said it merely put right an error in earlier legislation.

Leading the fight against the FedEx provision, Sen Edward Kennedy, D-Massachusetts, brought Senate action to a grinding halt by insisting on having the clerk read the whole 112-page bill, a task estimated to take more than four hours.

Republican Leader Trent Lott filed a motion to force action on the bill but under the rules a vote could not take place before Wednesday. Lott had said earlier he hoped the Senate could adjourn Monday night or Tuesday.

At issue was whether employees of FedEx were covered by the Railway Labour Act that required them to form a nationwide bargaining unit if they wish to have a union, or the National Labour Relations Act, which allowed local bargaining units.

A bill passed last year left the situation at FedEx ambiguous and the provision in the bill sought to ensure that the firm was covered by the Railway Labour Act, which made union organising more difficult.

Airline employees are covered by the Railway Labour Act, and FedEx's pilots are unionized. Truck drivers are usually covered by the Labour Relations Act, Sen. Kennedy said. FedEx's drivers are not unionized.
The Massachusetts Democrat attacked the provision in the bill as "a parting shot against American workers in the closing hours of this Congress."
Lott told reporters: "There's no doubt in my mind that this is labour trying to extract one additional pound of flesh from the Congress as we go out the door."
Lott would need 60 votes to cut off debate and Kennedy indicated that that he was not yet able to block Lott.
"We're building gathering strength. We haven't taken a head count," he said.

Kennedy suggested that the Senate could pass a separate resolution striking the FedEx provision and send it to the House, where members have already left town, to be adopted without debate. Lott said he did not believe the House wouild accept this course.
In a floor speech Kennedy said that FedEx "is notorious in its anti-union ideology, but there is no need for Congress to become an accomplice in its union-busting tactic."
He said the company's truck drivers in Pennsylvania had been trying to join the United Auto Workers union for two years.
FedEx spokswoman Shirlee Clark said the company needed the provision in the bill to resolve costly legal challenges resulting from ambiguous current law.
She said that a requirement that the firm's "couriers" be organised nationally was needed to prevent labour groups disrupting the firm's integrated air-ground operations.
